memories.title: A face built for power
memories.body:
The museum identifies this marble portrait as Constantine the Great. Its square face, large open eyes and distinctive fringe belong to an official imperial image. The catalog dates the head to 313–324 CE and records its height as 260 cm.

Found in the Basilica of Maxentius, the head survives apart from the colossal seated body. Read the face as a public image of power, not a candid likeness.
memories.cue: Find the face. Which emperor does the museum identify, and how tall is the surviving head?

memories.title: The finger is a later addition
memories.body:
The raised index finger is a modern addition to an ancient fragment. The museum says the original hand probably held a sceptre. That “probably” matters: the missing object is an interpretation.

The statue combined marble for exposed body parts with other materials for its clothed body. The seated pose evoked Jupiter. Remember the hand as a cue to separate surviving evidence from restoration.
memories.cue: Find the raised finger. Is it ancient or restored, and what did the hand probably hold?

memories.title: Barefoot, like a god
memories.body:
The museum describes the feet as more than two metres long. Constantine wears neither boots nor sandals in this statue: bare feet helped present the emperor like a god.

The two feet preserve different poses. One heel rises while the other foot rests flat. Metal pins and bars held the statue’s different materials together. This foot is a cue to reconstruct the seated body from surviving fragments.
memories.cue: Find the giant toes. Why was the emperor barefoot, and how long were the feet?

curatedTour.title: Fragments of an Emperor
curatedTour.subtitle: Rome · Three marble fragments tell a story of identity, restoration and power. Follow the stops, then test one detail through its object.
